summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for carrying uncompressed high-definition television as defined by the SMPTE 292M standard. SMPTE is the main standards body for motion imaging, and 292M defines a serial digital interface for HDTV transport inside a facility.

plainLanguage.summary: Studios use a special cable format for HD video. This note shows how to chop it into Internet packets and send it over a network.

questions: how to send hdtv over rtp
what is a pgroup in rtp video
why does smpte 292m rtp need a 32 bit sequence number
subtitle: How to carry studio-grade uncompressed HDTV video over RTP packets on an IP network.

tldr.problem: SMPTE 292M moves uncompressed HDTV between studio equipment over a dedicated serial link at 1.485 Gbps or 1.485/1.001 Gbps, and there was no standard way to send it across IP networks.
tldr.mechanism: Each SMPTE 292M line is split into one or more RTP packets, with a 4 octet payload header that extends the sequence number to 32 bits and carries the field flags and line number, and a 148.5 MHz RTP timestamp.
tldr.outcome: The flow has a constant high bit rate and cannot be congestion controlled, so the RFC says to use it only on private or resource-reserved networks.

today: RFC 3497 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RTP as specified in RFC 1889.

sections.title: Why Send SMPTE 292M Over RTP
sections.content:
The serial digital interface SMPTE 292M is a common way to move uncompressed High Definition Television (HDTV) between cameras, encoders, video tape recorders and other equipment. It uses 10 bit words and a total data rate of either 1.485 Gbps or 1.485/1.001 Gbps.

A dedicated cable suits a studio, but IP networks are widely available and have a lot of bandwidth. RFC 3497 therefore defines an RTP payload format for SMPTE 292M video. It covers only uncompressed HDTV. Compressed HDTV is a subset of MPEG-2, and the RFC says RFC 2250 already describes its transport over RTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Studios move HD pictures down a special cable. This note lets the same picture ride on the Internet, which is already everywhere.

sections.title: How a SMPTE 292M Line Is Built
sections.content:
A SMPTE 292M television line is two interleaved streams: one of luminance (Y) samples and one of chrominance (CrCb) values. Each stream has four parts: a start of active video timing reference (SAV), the digital active line, an end of active video timing reference (EAV), and digital line blanking. Ancillary data can take the place of blanking or of the active line.

SAV and EAV each begin with three 10 bit words, 0x3FF 0x000 0x000, followed by an XYZ word with flags. The F flag says whether the line belongs to field 1 or field 2, and the V flag marks field blanking. After EAV come two words, LN0 and LN1, which carry an 11 bit line number, and two CRC words.

The format of the active line and blanking is set by source format documents such as SMPTE 260M, 295M, 274M and 296M. The RFC transfers the 292M stream whatever the source format is.
sections.plainLanguage: A TV picture is drawn one line at a time. Each line has a start marker, the picture part, an end marker with the line number, and a quiet gap.

sections.title: Payload Design
sections.content:
Each SMPTE 292M data line goes into one or more RTP packets, including timing signals, blanking levels, active lines and ancillary data. The SAV and the EAV+LN+CRC signals MUST NOT be fragmented across packets, because the decoder uses them to find the start of scan lines.

The standard RTP header is followed by a 4 octet payload header. The marker (M) bit in the RTP header marks the packet holding the last sample of a video frame.

The payload header adds 16 bits to the 16 bit RTP sequence number, making it 32 bits. At 1.485 Gbps with packets of at least a thousand octets, the 32 bit number wraps in about 6 hours, while a 16 bit one would wrap in 336 milliseconds. The RTP timestamp runs at 148.5 MHz (or 148.5/1.001 MHz), so every 10 bit word has its own timestamp; the 32 bit value wraps in 21 seconds. The payload header also repeats the 11 bit line number, which helps if the packet containing the EAV is lost.
sections.plainLanguage: Every line of the picture goes into one or more parcels, and the start and end markers are never split. The parcel numbers are made extra long so they do not run out within a second.

sections.title: Packet Layout and Pixel Groups
sections.content:
After the RTP header and 4 octet payload header comes the SMPTE 292M data. The RTP header uses a dynamically allocated payload type, a marker bit set to 1 on the last packet of a frame, and the low 16 bits of the sequence number. The other fields are used as usual.

The payload header holds the high 16 bits of the sequence number, the F and V bits copied from the SMPTE 292M timing signals, a 2 bit Z field that SHOULD be zero and MUST be ignored by receivers, and the line number of the first 10 bit word in the packet.

To keep video octet aligned without splitting related luminance and chrominance values, the RFC defines a pgroup. The active line SHOULD NOT be fragmented within a pgroup. A pgroup of 1 octet means the data may be split at any octet boundary, which is useful when the source format is not known. Typical 4:2:2 sources need a pgroup of 5 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Pixels are packed in little bundles, and a bundle is never torn in half between two parcels. A small header on each parcel says which line of the picture it starts on.

sections.title: RTCP, MIME Type and SDP
sections.content:
For RTCP, the RFC applies the rules of RFC 1889: RTCP bandwidth limited to 5% of the data rate and a minimum average interval of 5 seconds between RTCP packets. With this data rate the minimum interval governs. The sender's octet count in SR packets wraps in 23 seconds and the cumulative packets lost wraps in 93 seconds, so applications that need the real totals must count the rollovers themselves.

The RFC registers the media type video/SMPTE292M. The required parameter rate is the RTP clock rate, 148500000 Hz or 148500000/1.001 Hz; for the latter, a timestamp value of 148351648 MUST be used. The optional pgroup parameter defaults to 1 octet. In SDP, the stream is announced with an rtpmap line and a fmtp line carrying pgroup.
sections.plainLanguage: The note also says how to count parcels for health reports and how to describe the stream in a sign-up message, because the counters would roll over in seconds.

sections.title: Security and Network Limits
sections.content:
The bandwidth of 1.485 Gbps without RTP overhead is high enough to cause denial of service if sent onto most Internet paths. Since congestion control is not possible for SMPTE 292M over RTP, use of the payload SHOULD be narrowly limited to suitably connected endpoints, or networks with QoS guarantees.

If QoS is used, receivers SHOULD monitor packet loss to check they get the service requested. With best-effort service, receivers MUST monitor loss and MUST leave the session if the loss rate is too high. A rate is acceptable if a TCP flow on the same path would get at least the same average throughput.

The RFC also says the format does not create uneven receiver processing cost that could be used for denial of service, and refers to the security considerations of RTP and its profiles.
sections.plainLanguage: This stream is like a firehose that never slows down, so it should only be used on pipes built for it. If the pipe is too crowded, the viewer must walk away.

data.title: SDP mapping
data.code:
m=video 30000 RTP/AVP 111
a=rtpmap:111 SMPTE292M/148500000
a=fmtp:111  pgroup=5
